query: Which method can be used for phase stability, microstructure refinement, and property optimization, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Implementing a CALPHAD-based high-throughput computational screening method in the design of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) will lead to improved phase stability, refined microstructures, and enhanced material properties compared to conventionally designed alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: A multi-principal element high-entropy alloy system that initially shows a mixture of phases and possible elemental segregation.
generation.intervention: Application of the CALPHAD method integrated with high-throughput calculations and multi-objective optimization algorithms.
generation.conditions: Processing within defined compositional ranges (e.g., 5–50 at.% for each element) and operating at various temperature conditions; using computational resources capable of parallel processing to manage large data sets.
generation.structural_mediator: Phase diagram predictions and thermophysical parameters (such as enthalpy of mixing, atomic size differences, and the omega parameter) generated via CALPHAD calculations.
generation.mechanism: CALPHAD uses established thermodynamic databases and models to simulate phase equilibria through free-energy minimization. This simulation helps identify the conditions under which a predominant single-phase solid solution is formed, guiding microstructure refinement and resulting in optimized mechanical or functional properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: HEAs designed using this CALPHAD-based approach will exhibit a dominant single-phase microstructure with fewer undesired intermetallics, leading to improved mechanical and functional properties relative to alloys developed without such computational guidance.
generation.baseline: Alloys designed via traditional empirical methods may require extensive trial-and-error and exhibit multi-phase regions with less controlled microstructural refinement and suboptimal properties.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness is limited by the quality and availability of accurate thermodynamic databases and may become a computational challenge for systems with more than five principal elements.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of improvements in phase stability and properties remains uncertain and is dependent on database accuracy and processing specifics.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEAs with comparable base compositions: one set designed using CALPHAD-based high-throughput screening and optimization, and one set developed using traditional empirical guidelines. Process both sets under identical conditions. Analyze the phase composition via X-ray diffraction, assess the microstructure using electron microscopy (SEM/TEM), and measure mechanical properties such as tensile strength and hardness.
measurements: X-ray diffraction patterns to determine phase purity and detect intermetallic phases
SEM/TEM images for microstructure assessment and elemental segregation analysis
Mechanical property data including tensile strength and hardness measurements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the CALPHAD-designed alloys do not show statistically significant improvements in phase stability (i.e., a more dominant single-phase region), microstructure refinement, or enhanced mechanical properties compared to the traditionally designed alloys, then the hypothesis is considered falsified.

The design stage of the quinary HEA started with the calculation of the thermophysical parameters, mainly enthalpy of mixing (∆ H mix ), entropy of mixing ( Δ S mix ), atomic size difference ( δ ), and the omega parameter ( Ω ) for several compositions. The ability of a material to form a single-phase was empirically shown to depend on these three parameters. For that, the value for Δ H mix was recommended to be in the range of −15 to 5 kJ per mole, while δ should be smaller than 6.6 and Ω larger than 1.1 [26] , [27] . ∆ H mix , δ , and Ω were then calculated using Eqs. 1 – 4 respectively. Other theoretical parameters such as density ( ρ ), melting temperature ( T m ), and VEC were calculated using the rule of mixture, as shown in Eq. 5 , where i represents the element type, X represents the property, r is the atomic radius, and c represents the concentration of element i .

The atomic radii and enthalpy used in the calculations are taken from refs. [28] , [29] , respectively. The concept of HEAs provides us an unprecedented degree of freedom in the design of advanced alloys with promising properties. For the rapid exploration of the vast compositional space and investigation of the composition and temperature effects on the microstructure, advanced HEA-design strategies and efficient tools are necessary. At present, a few advanced HEA-design strategies were reported by combining the physicochemical criteria, CALPHAD, data mining, and multi-objective optimization algorithm [21] , [22] , [35] – [37] , demonstrating that the CALPHAD method has played an important role in the design of advanced HEAs. There are two essential requirements to carry out calculations, using the CALPHAD method: computational software and database.

The computational software could significantly affect the efficiency of HTC since massive calculations are carried out. In the example of the Al–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ti quinary system, it takes only a few hours on a desktop computer to finish the HTCs (~ 3 × 10 3 ) within the composition range of 5–50 at.% for each element and finally screen out eight potential alloys.
